comments.text:
Okay so check it out, 11900k 2% bottleneck with a 9070 xt at 4k
Looks like this will be my new combo for a 4K desktop, soon. 
I will OC away the bottleneck. 11TH gen allows a good processing, for most things.

I can do a processor, GPU and PSU swap with a SSD upgrade and that will be over a grand in upgrades, but will effectively renew my PC.
Can sell the GPU and processor I use now, some parts and a older tower. 

I have peripherals not messing with little kid stuff, a 4090 or something is dumb for your 1080p FPS rig lmao.
My system is based on using peripherals for a lot of things, not a GPU ina box.
Many systems are what I call bare bones GPU style. 
It's the little things that matter, the desk and the keyboard, the screen, the mic and pole.
I have a good chair, audio system, glass mousepads and a lot of extras that make it feel better.

Cable management, I spent over 800$ I think. Wanna know how I did this ?. 
3X usb hubs, a Furman, Denon, 2 XL steel troughs, 4 plastic troughs, extension cables and cables.
Otherwise, would be a mistake. Nothing is visible and is the cleanest thing ever, cable wise.
You gonna stick your head under the table, no.

 I get full use of 1 tower, normally you would use a second tower, 
for two workstations but this is a nono, just do the cable route with the hubs. I have a flush mount hub and a mic boom with USB hub at the bottom.
The pole can hold lights, camera, and the pole is necessity, not a boom scissor arm. I needed a pneumatic arm and pole.
I ended using a light boom. 

Need the booms, the right kind. The pole is a good idea and you can get a 4ft tube and light the front.
So the looks of your geek setup are all wrong, sorry.

Your booms are stuff are wrong + extras.
remember booms are for lights, poles are for serious things.
You guys sold me the wrong stuff really. 

LOL..smh online reviews are so bad.
I needed to do everything myself, nothing I got was reviewed
I had to find and test it, myself.

The metal desk, add ons, the mounts are all good now, wall mounts.
If you don't use a wall mount, your monitors are too low, or use a pole. 
You want 10 inches of space underneath or more for your eye level.

Most setups monitor stands or mounts, not ideally setup.
My lamp needs to be where it is, nothing would work otherwise.
My chairs need to be where they are and desks. I had no options for screen placement
Everything is powder coat black, no color options for my desk.

I had no option for tower placement, mic placement, speaker.
no option where to put my console or even my lunchbox headphone and mic amp.
0 option where to put hubs or keyboards, wires, everything was predetermined.
I have the option to plug and play anything, expand and add devices and instruments.
You can just plug in your turntable in, your robot.

I am pretty sure your setup wants to be like mine, cause it's how to stretch a tower to maximum production
and you get a 2 person workstation that can produce anything, audio or professional audio or video.
Streaming is simple. I have all the programs installed, I need.
I use Abelton and Adobe software, no problems.
 
It looks good too, but you guys don't even come over.
I did this for a reason cause it's the future of how you need the office studio.
Just get two desks and load all the i/o's of your tower.

You guys just have not figured out the future layout, is this one. I planned it that much and there's no better option.
Every home should have this now. I have space for sticks, pads or controllers, heck I can play cards or eat on my desk or walk on it.

You don't want that cheap stuff, threw away multiple chairs n desks.
You and your wife can share a PC, while being somewhat together and you know, not having 2 PC's.
It's the future of compact studios, one processor per room is what you need.

Even the glass pads I got for the center, this is important for the surface cause the other surface is garbage.
Powder coat black is basically the way to go, for all metal surfaces.

For decoration, I have nothin, absolutely nothing but light in my tower. I have a little fast charger robot on my desk, that's it. 
Otherwise my desk is cleared out. I have a Razer mouse in a case behind the curved screen just cause nothing can fit there.
On the reverse side, a 5G modem that is around the same size, it's like 500$, I had to made this black, so I used some black tape skin and it's so much better.
I have soooo much open desk space still, I keep knick knaacks on custom shelves, not on the desk.

The idea is you get a large interface like Mbox studio, nice Preamp like a Apollo or Focusright box, and that's your audio system.
You plug a mic into the and box, then run two short patch cables over to the line in, connect the two boxes in a series.

Plus USB C interface to motherboard I.O. The two boxes sit against the back wall, while you can turn the knobs and adjust everything.
This gives you so many inputs and outputs. Like a lot of extra headphones, instruments. So I will have all audio connectivity, all USB connectivity options minus thunderbolt and I don't need Dante.
Ridiculous amount of inputs and outputs total.

Yeah the audio boxes are about a grand for both, little more. Can VERY easily get the wrong boxes, again no options.
This is if you want a nice, working and professional level studio room that is clean, orderly and up to electrical code.
I had no options for a different anything, power strips, nothing is going to work here except what I have.

Studio desks are made for old, outdated systems. All you need is a rack space, at most.
I didn't need a rack space. You can just get the preamp for the desk and the rack would be off to the side
You can bring a small rack here, plug it in. Converters are the same. I think the two box system is the way to go for a modern little studio,
run short patch cables. You will have excellent audio, makes your speakers better and headphones.

If you need pro level audio, the mic will run through it so it's like really good quality.
You guys probably use it in your studio, or maybe not...what do you use for audio mics ?
I do music and wanted to make a all in one workstation that would handle anything you could create on PC.

This is what you guys need for home, buy things to last and then keep it well maintained, you can stop upgrading and produce at home.
Your other options are costly and useless. I spent a few grand, no big deal. All planning and reading, talking.
Impossible without a plan.

comments.text:
Why is GPU Userbenchmarks write this message under an AMD card comparison? 

If you are considering an AMD 9000 series GPU because you have been influenced by Reddit, Twitter or a wealthy tech YouTuber, it’s worth understanding AMD’s track record. While their GPUs are often great at beating cherry-picked benchmarks, they normally fall short in real-world gaming performance. Every year, an army of influencers target first-time buyers declaring AMD a godsend for PC gamers. Every year a small percentage of users get duped. Since almost all PC gamers use Steam, the February 2025 Steam statistics are relevant: AMD’s combined market share for discrete 5000/6000/7000 series GPUs is 3%. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s 4060 alone has 9% market share. This reality starkly contrasts with influencer hype. The reason is simple: influencers rarely play games and gamers rarely buy AMD GPUs. Experienced gamers know all too well that high average fps are worthless when they are accompanied with stutters, random crashes, black screens, excessive noise and a limited feature set. It’s notable that AMD’s GPUs have not historically had these problems in consoles because, unlike PCs, consoles operate in a closed environment which is less dependent on robust drivers. Using influencers for hardware performance data is less effective than using foxes to babysit chickens.

comments.text: They 100% made the 9070 and it's XT variant for 1440p gaming. All these 2160p comparisons don't do a GPU that's made for 1440p any justice. The goodest boy, 1080 Ti, can run 1440p, but no one ever tries to run it at 1440p, because it was designed to run at 1080p. Hell, the 2080 Super can run games at 2160p, but no one ever does because it was designed for 1080p. Also, the 70 in the name means it's a mid-range card, just like NVIDIA does. That means, AMD can get even spicier with their 9000 series. If they came out with a 9090 and XT variant with 24Gb of VRAM,  THEN you can have a comparison to a 4090, and 5090, because then it would be a card designed to run at 2160p at 60fps or higher like we all want, but don't have the money for. Keep this in mind, 8-12Gb of VRAM is for 1080p, 12-16Gb of VRAM is for 1440p, and 16-24Gb of VRAM is for 2160p. I love the fact that AMD is targeting 1440p. 1440p got skipped over and everyone is suffering with GPU prices because of 2160p and we as the consumer let it happen! I completely understand (and actually love) that gamers are able to get "mostly" affordable cards, even if they'll be flying off shelves, and scalped for a slightly higher cost, at least for a long while, but AMD just doesn't seem to want to "beat" Nvidia, and that's really a shame. AMD has come SO far in the CPU world, where, for many many years, they were almost completely out done by Intel (Except in the case of workstation, but I'm talking about gamers here.) and now AMD is even starting to hold dominance in the CPU world, even over Intel, which I absolutely LOVE to see, because MORE competition makes the market BETTER, and drives larger improvements from all sides. The problem, is that, from what I've seen last generation, and this generation, is that AMD just wants to be the affordable, but not quite "amazing" card. They just want to be the average card, that isn't as good, but more people have access to it. I don't like that, because, ultimately, at the end of the day, everyone 'wants' the top of the line Nvidia card. If every gamer were given an unlimited budget for a gaming rig, they'd almost all surely buy the 5090 right now, and that kinda sucks, because while Nvidia sits atop the mountain of performance, AMD doesn't seem to be making a run for the crown, and that makes a stagnant market. It really ultimately hurts both AMD and Nvidia in this case, because Nvidia (As we've seen with both the 40 and 50 series) have been having some serious issues, with the power connectors, and horrible, horrible launches, making an $2,000 MSRP card almost immediately cost $5,000. I want to see AMD make a REAL card. A card that REALLY shoots for the top, EVEN if it comes at a much higher price tag. I want to see AMD make Nvidia sweat. Make Nvidia nervous. comments.text:
9:47 Seems like the fps limits are borked for DLSS, you probably should disable gsync and vsync and disable fps limit when doing a framegen test.
There are some games where the fps limits don't work correctly or do their own thing.
For example in Monster Hunter Wilds, while you never enabled framegen, fps limits works correctly.
But if you enable framegen, then in game fps limit 60 will equal to 120 of total fps, also that's how it's listed in the config.ini file. When you disable framegen it limits to what you see.
But with gpu driver fps limit you have to set it based on the total fps instead of real fps, and when you disable framegen, then it will break and limit to half of the value instead so if you have a 120 fps limit in gpu drivers it will be 60 instead, until you restart the game and don't toggle framegen on and off on next run.
In 1 game I had to set in drivers to 180 fps limit, so I could get 90 fps limit in the game, otherwise the 90 fps limit limited to 45 instead, regardless if framegen was on or not.
The in game fps limits seem to be so far reverse of gpu driver fps limits, if they're bugged or don't describe properly what they're doing.
In indiana jones for example, while you're in the menus, the framegen doesn't even work until you close out of the menu, so you might be sometimes like is it even working, or is some fps limit nonsense going on.

After staying up super late and waking up super early, spamming online stores for inventory to appear and subsequently attempting to purchase a couple different $600 9070XT models only to receive an out-of-stock notification during processing, I was finally able to purchase the “GIGABYTE Gaming Radeon RX 9070 XT 16GB GDDR6 PCI Express 5.0 x16 Graphcis Card GV-R9070XTGAMING OC-16GD.” 
Yesterday I set up a Trade-in for my current GPU in preparation for the upgrade. My transaction was completed this morning (3/6/2025) prior to 8:30AM Central Time. 
I received three emails from NewEgg this morning:
1. 8:29AM “We received your Trade-in Form”
2. 8:59AM “Order confirmed: Newegg order #577… (1 item)
3. 9:05AM “Order cancelled due to insufficient stock”
Apparently, it took NewEgg 30 full minutes to process my order. By that time—unbeknownst to me—my GPU was sold to another customer (possibly someone who did not have a trade-in offer). Meanwhile, I went about my day, thinking that I had secured my GPU and allowing 100% of all 9070XT models to be depleted. So now I have no GPU coming, and I have the pleasure of hoping NewEgg will honor the purchase agreement so that I won’t have to pay an additional $100 (who knows?) whenever inventory is replenished.

comments.text:
The raw BOM cost of the 9070XT is basically no more than the BOM cost of the 7800XT which had an MSRP of $499 and regularly sold for $450. Sure I get that 4nm is ever so slightly more expensive than 5nm but at the same time GDDR6 prices have come down, other costs like shipping and general inflation might have also increased but I think AMD could have been more aggressive if they really really wanted to, but $599 in the current climate of basically 'no competition from Nvidia' is good enough and will sell very well. The 5070Ti is certainly not worth $300-400 more than the 9070XT, but AMD needs to be really careful because if Nvidia sorts themselves out (this could happen if it's yield issues or something else we don't know) and start to fill shelves with $749 cards then 100% AMD can not look to charge $650-700+ for this card which has been rumoured once all the MSRP cards are sold. 
The 5070Ti is better in every single way, but it's just not '$300 better', but most buyers including myself would happy pay $50-100 more for better overall performance, better power usage, better ray tracing, better and wider DLSS support, Reflex, HDR, better encoding quality, better support in content creation apps, Cuda, the list goes on. I genuinely had my heart set on a 5070Ti this year (I've not owned Nvidia in about 20 years!) but the performance increase wasn't that impressive and the pricing/available is just ridiculous. Thankfully AMD looks to have got their sh!t together this generation, it's a solid card, decent performance, they are addressing their shortcomings and they have currently priced this card where it needs to be in the market we have right now. But honestly, AMD can't go north of $600 long term as this card simply isn't good enough against a $749 5070Ti, imo.

comments.text:
I feel like we're seeing a split in the market where NVIDIA is going all-in on the industrial AI market and leaving gaming out of it due to the higher margins in the AI space due to a market rush.

AMD seems to be saying "okay we'll put just enough AI investment in to match NVIDIA's feature set, but we're going to focus on rendering performance and encoding."

It's honestly a good thing since that means the better gaming and video workstation cards are going to be less affected by the AI drought we're seeing. Let NVIDIA move away from the market and expand the potential market share for Intel and AMD.

Intel having a motivation to try and make an enthusiast card will be really good for the market; AMD backing out of the enthusiast market might be a bit of a red herring given that they'll still be putting out workstation cards of equivalent performance. I suspect if Intel actually made a gaming-capable enthusiast card AMD would quickly re-spec a W series to get a 32gb monster out (that would cost like $2,700 but hey, it'd beat the 5090 in 8k performance with that massive VRAM.

comments.text:
I would like to bring up what a different YouTuber (I can't remember who) brought up in a short: Using an older HDMI and Display Port spec REALLY does not matter on this mid-tier of graphics cards. That YouTuber made the point that, at this price point and performance level, these cards are not going to put out the frame rates in most games to truly utilize the full bandwidth of the new HDMI and Display Port standards, so why sweat that detail? And that is a valid point, if you have the money for a high refresh rate, super high end 4K display that requires the newer versions of those ports, you are not wasting your time and money on looking at let alone buying a RTX 5070 Ti or an AMD Radeon RX 9070 XT, and even the RTX 4080-5080. Those people go straight to the new Titan series cards of the current era, the RTX 4090-5090 cards, when they can find them. To me, without using the gimmicks, AMD has closed the gap hugely on Nvidia in the mid-tier. And, IF the price points stick even remotely close to MSRP, I would be happy to upgrade from my RTX 2080 Super to a Radeon RX 9070 XT, versus either a RTX 5080 or 5070 Ti. I don't need 4K gaming, and AMD just made a card with enough rasterization performance to play 99.9% of my game collection just fine maxed out at 2560x1440 and 100Hz, for $600.00 MSRP. It would do ray tracing in the games I have with it as an option WAY better than my current card, and I would never need to touch FSR. I can't care about newer games right now, there is nothing out or coming in the near future that I care to own, when I have a collection now I can never hope to complete.

 TL:DR Bravo to AMD for finally making a mid-tier card to compete with Nvidia, and under cut their stupidity and lies. If pricing stays stable (doubt it) I just may have to finally upgrade again, and back to an all AMD configuration.

comments.text:
The only thing AMD needs to do now is refine their drivers and get better support from developers. I had a 7700 XT, and while it worked great in most cases, it struggled in some niche areas I actually enjoy—areas where my old 1080 Ti had no issues.

One major problem I encountered was with Steam Link and other home streaming services like Parsec and Moonlight. The 7700 XT has a known issue where streaming will freeze (though the game itself keeps running), forcing you to restart the stream. This happened anywhere from once an hour to every 10 minutes, which was incredibly frustrating.

Another issue was with Diablo 4. Many users, including myself, reported that after a loading screen, the game would show a black screen with only the UI elements, making it unplayable. On top of that, I experienced serious stuttering and freezing, which Diablo 4 is known for, but it was way worse on my 7700 XT compared to my 1080 Ti.

I also had problems with Hogwarts Legacy and Elden Ring. Something—either RTX or FSR, I’m not sure which—bugged out, causing serious stuttering and screen blinking. I suspect it was a combination of FSR, RTX, and faulty drivers, because after a driver update, the issue disappeared.

Speaking of drivers, I had the 7700 XT for 3–4 months, and in that time, I only saw one driver update. Meanwhile, NVIDIA releases driver updates so frequently it’s almost annoying.

After dealing with all of this, I finally gave up, sold the 7700 XT, and bought a 4070 Super—and honestly, I’m pretty happy with it.

comments.text:
The problem with the high end GPU for AMD was Navi41 and Navi42 failed on the first implementation too late into the design phase.  The problem was fixed for UDNA (RDNA5), but AMD wouldn't be able to fix Navi41 and Navi42 in a reasonable time.  The only way AMD can deliver a "high end" GPU is if AMD had sufficient work done for a non-leaked chip, like Navi43 for example, that was designed similar to Navi31's single compute die + multiple memory controller dies.  The rumors of a 32GB "gaming" card could be anything from a special Navi48 die with double VRAM, dual Navi48, or AMD had work on another RDNA4 die that wasn't leaked.  If AMD had a back-up high end GPU, why not push it instead of Navi48?  AMD expected the RTX 50 series to be great, and thus such a chip still would not make sense.  Regardless of such speculation, the best chance for an RDNA4 high end GPU is a mid-generation release, if AMD thinks it is viable.  Given that stores need supply and how much hardware troubles Nvidia is having for their RTX 50 series launch, conditions may "now" be viable for the back-up high end RDNA4 GPU.

Given how badly the RTX 50 series launched, will these problems influence how soon or how late the RTX 60 series comes?  Jensen should be upset with how much the entire internet is mocking his CES presentation of the RTX 50 series.  It is too late to unlaunch the RTX 50 series and delay it 6 months to fix everything.  Not only should Nvidia be fixing the RTX 50 series, they need to evaluate the risk that the RTX 60 series could repeat all of these mishaps.

Positive POV: It's 150 dollars cheaper than the 5070ti, it has improved raytracing, solid performance per dollar, actually in stock, solid AI catchup to Nvidia and it beats the standard 5070 in performance for basically the same price.

Negative POV: It still struggles in the one market AMD has decided to place all their cards in, the mid-range. It doesn't even beat Nvidia in Nvidia's weakest generational uplift yet. If there ever was a chance for AMD to catch up or beat Nvidia in performance, this was it. This was their chance, but they just couldn't do it. It draws a lot more power then the 5070ti, still sits 8-19% behind Nvidia in raytracing and they are absolutely cooked if Nvidia drops prices anywhere close to 600.

comments.text:
Who is out there running text generation using ONNX with DirectML??? I get you want to get a CUDA agnostic benchmark, but there is no way that a 4070 Ti with half the memory bandwidth of a 7900XTX manages almost double the performance in text generation in any real world scenario.

edit: edit: RED FLAG! I looked up the UL Procyon documentation, their scoring formula and which quants they are running. Now if they use INT4 with sparsity, then these test favor nVidia... except the 7900XTX has so much more raw FP16 and memory bandwidth, its AI TOPS should be competitive in dense INT4 compared to the 4070 and 3080. Yet they lose horribly. Why? Their scoring equation divides a "constant value" by the time to first token to calculate their "score" —if time to first token takes dozens of seconds to minutes, then maybe this would be a balanced test, but it don't—it takes less then 1 second across all their prompt, it's basically a multiplier, because they use a very small context window (2k) while their entire phi-3.5 benchmark take maybe 1-2 minutes in total to complete 7 prompts. 

GPU A (*cough*4090*cough*) can complete the Phi-3.5-mini benchmark is less than 50 seconds, with a average TTFT of around 0.25s, scoring 5000 points! But if GPU B has an average TTFT of 0.50s (adding 1.75 seconds total in the full benchmark); this would instantly halve their score. GPU B would have to generate double the tokens/s and complete the test in half the time to overcome this discrepancy in (memory) latency to get an equal score, despite being obviously better in such a case.

To give you an idea of how much this TTFT part of their scoring equation biases the test, and another major RED FLAG, is the 9070 score; RDNA4 should perform 4-8 times better in int4 OPs than RDNA3 architecturally, and the 9070's have more AI TOPS than the 5070's. They should generating more tokens/second in theory, especially in a benchmark that isn't using CUDA. How much more? About 50%. Yet, it's the 5070's that score 50% higher! And they lose to the 7900 XTX also. The only advantage the XTX have over the 9070 is higher memory bandwidth, yet memory bandwidth doesn't seem to determine the outcome of this benchmark anywhere else.
